title: Ship sk as a tool
summary: Pack Sidekick as a .NET tool, install it with dotnet tool install, and have sk check its own settings.

steps.title: From dotnet run to sk
body: So far you start Sidekick with `dotnet run -- standup` inside its folder. Today it becomes a real command: type `sk` in **any** terminal, in any folder, like `git` or `dotnet`.
.NET calls that a **tool**: a console app packed as a NuGet package and installed by the `dotnet` command. Four settings in `sk.csproj` make your Sidekick one:
```xml
<PropertyGroup>
<OutputType>Exe</OutputType>                <!-- a program, not a library -->
<PackAsTool>true</PackAsTool>               <!-- dotnet pack builds a tool package -->
<ToolCommandName>sk</ToolCommandName>       <!-- the command people type -->
<PackageId>Sidekick.Dojo</PackageId>        <!-- the name dotnet tool install asks for -->
<Version>1.0.0</Version>                    <!-- bump it for every new release -->
</PropertyGroup>
Your Sidekick's template already has them. In this lesson you learn what each one does, install it for real, and write `sk doctor`'s check so a broken setting is caught before you ship.

steps.prompt: Match each `sk.csproj` setting to what it controls.
pairs: the name you pass to `dotnet tool install`

steps.prompt: You change `<ToolCommandName>sk</ToolCommandName>` to `<ToolCommandName>sidekick</ToolCommandName>`, pack and install again. What do you type now?
steps.explain: The command name comes from `ToolCommandName`. `PackageId` is only the package's name, used by `dotnet tool install`, `update` and `uninstall`.

steps.title: Pack it, install it, update it
body: From your Sidekick's folder (Builds > Sidekick > **Open as a Code space**, or the unzipped download):
```text
dotnet pack                                                  builds ./nupkg/Sidekick.Dojo.1.0.0.nupkg
dotnet tool install -g Sidekick.Dojo --add-source ./nupkg    installs the sk command for your user
sk --version                                                 works in any terminal from now on
- `-g` (global) puts the command in `%USERPROFILE%\.dotnet\tools`, which the .NET installer added to your `PATH`. Open a **new** terminal if `sk` is not found yet.
- `--add-source ./nupkg` tells `dotnet` to look in your folder as well as nuget.org.
- After a change: bump `<Version>`, `dotnet pack` again, then `dotnet tool update -g Sidekick.Dojo --add-source ./nupkg`.
- `dotnet tool list -g` shows what is installed; `dotnet tool uninstall -g Sidekick.Dojo` removes it.
Your data stays where it always was, in `%USERPROFILE%\.sidekick`, so the installed `sk` sees the tasks you added with `dotnet run`.

steps.prompt: Arrange the commands to release version 1.1.0 of an `sk` that is already installed, then check it.
steps.explain: Bump the version first, so the new package is newer than the installed one; pack it; update from your folder; then check what runs.

steps.prompt: `dotnet tool install -g` succeeded, but your open terminal says `sk` is not recognized. What is the most likely fix?
options: Open a new terminal so it picks up the updated PATH (`%USERPROFILE%\.dotnet\tools`)
steps.explain: A terminal reads `PATH` when it starts. Tools go into `%USERPROFILE%\.dotnet\tools`; a new terminal (or a restart of your editor) sees them.

steps.title: The next version number
prompt: `dotnet tool update` only installs a package that is newer, so every release bumps `Version`. Versions follow *semantic versioning*: `major.minor.patch`.
Write `static string NextVersion(string version, string bump)`:
- `bump` (ignore case and spaces) is `patch` (1.2.3 -> 1.2.4), `minor` (1.2.3 -> 1.3.0) or `major` (1.2.3 -> 2.0.0); anything else throws `ArgumentException`.
- `version` (trimmed) must be exactly three whole numbers separated by dots, otherwise throw `FormatException`.
- The parts are numbers: `1.9.9` minor is `1.10.0`.
starter: static string NextVersion(string version, string bump)
solution: static string NextVersion(string version, string bump)
if (parts.Length != 3) throw new FormatException($"\"{version}\" is not major.minor.patch");
throw new FormatException($"\"{parts[i]}\" is not a version number");
_ => throw new ArgumentException($"Unknown bump \"{bump}\": use major, minor or patch"),
template: Dojo.Eq("bump ignores case and spaces", "1.0.1", NextVersion(" 1.0.0 ", " Patch "));
hints: `version.Trim().Split('.')` must give exactly 3 parts; parse each with `int.TryParse`.
A switch expression on `bump.Trim().ToLowerInvariant()` picks the new text; the `_` arm throws.

steps.title: Reading a project file
body: A `.csproj` is XML. `System.Xml.Linq` reads it in two lines, wherever the setting sits:
```csharp fragment
var project = XDocument.Parse(xml);
string? packAsTool = project.Descendants("PackAsTool").FirstOrDefault()?.Value.Trim();
- `Descendants(name)` finds elements with that name at **any** depth (a project can have several `PropertyGroup`s).
- `FirstOrDefault()` is `null` when the setting is missing, so `?.` keeps the line safe; `.Value` is the text inside.
`sk doctor` reads the `sk.csproj` built into your Sidekick and lists anything that would stop it from installing.

steps.prompt: Complete the line so `name` is the text of the first `ToolCommandName`, or `null` when there is none.
steps.explain: `First()` would throw when the setting is missing; `FirstOrDefault()` gives `null`, which the `?.` turns into a `null` name.

steps.title: Use it for real: sk --version
prompt: Time to run your own Sidekick. Open it from **Builds > Sidekick > Open as a Code space** (or install it with the commands above) and run:
```text
dotnet run -- --version        or, once installed:   sk --version
dotnet run -- doctor

Paste the first line that `--version` printed between the quotes below and run the checks. (It starts with `sk 1.0`. Until you finish this lesson's last step it is just `sk 1.0.0`; after it, it also names your .NET version and data folder.)

tests.name: It is the line sk --version printed

hints: In the Code space terminal: `dotnet run -- --version`.
Copy the whole line, starting with `sk 1.0`, into the quotes.

steps.title: sk doctor and sk --version
prompt: **Sidekick piece: `sk doctor` and `sk --version`.** Milestone: **installed**. Write:
1. `static string VersionLine(string version, string runtime, string dataDir)` returning `sk {version} on .NET {runtime}, data in {dataDir}`.
2. `static List<string> ToolProblems(string csprojXml)`: parse the XML with `XDocument` and check, **in this order**, adding exactly these messages:
| Check | Message |
| `OutputType` is `Exe` | `OutputType must be Exe: a tool is a program` |
| `PackAsTool` is `true` (any case) | `PackAsTool must be true` |
| `ToolCommandName` present and not blank | `ToolCommandName is missing: it is the command people type` |
| `PackageId` present and not blank | `PackageId is missing: dotnet tool install needs a package name` |
| `Version` parses with `System.Version.TryParse` | `Version must look like 1.2.0` |
Settings can be in any `PropertyGroup`; trim their text. An empty list means ready to ship. `using System.Xml.Linq;` is in place.
starter: static string VersionLine(string version, string runtime, string dataDir)
solution: static string VersionLine(string version, string runtime, string dataDir) =>
if (Setting("OutputType") != "Exe") problems.Add("OutputType must be Exe: a tool is a program");
if (!string.Equals(Setting("PackAsTool"), "true", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase)) problems.Add("PackAsTool must be true");
if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(Setting("ToolCommandName"))) problems.Add("ToolCommandName is missing: it is the command people type");
if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(Setting("PackageId"))) problems.Add("PackageId is missing: dotnet tool install needs a package name");
if (Setting("Version") is not { } v || !System.Version.TryParse(v, out _)) problems.Add("Version must look like 1.2.0");

Dojo.Eq("a project ready to ship has no problems", new List<string>(), ToolProblems(dojoGood));
Dojo.Eq("PackAsTool True (any case) is fine", new List<string>(), ToolProblems(dojoGood.Replace("<PackAsTool>true", "<PackAsTool>True")));
Dojo.Eq("a plain console project: four problems, in order",
"ToolCommandName is missing: it is the command people type",

Dojo.Eq("a library cannot be a tool", new List<string> { "OutputType must be Exe: a tool is a program" }, ToolProblems(dojoGood.Replace(">Exe<", ">Library<")));
Dojo.Eq("PackAsTool false", new List<string> { "PackAsTool must be true" }, ToolProblems(dojoGood.Replace("<PackAsTool>true", "<PackAsTool>false")));

require.message: Finds settings at any depth with Descendants

hints: A local helper keeps it short: `string? Setting(string name) => project.Descendants(name).FirstOrDefault()?.Value.Trim();`.
The version check: `if (Setting("Version") is not { } v || !System.Version.TryParse(v, out _)) problems.Add(...);`.
steps.explain: Run `sk doctor` and `sk --version` in your Sidekick now. Then `dotnet pack` and `dotnet tool install -g Sidekick.Dojo --add-source ./nupkg`: from today `sk` works in every terminal you open.
